source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's Lebanon campus is the largest published power figure of any data center mapped in Ohio, at 35 MW across 400,000 square feet, in a state where only 9 of 79 mapped facilities publish a megawatt figure at all.

That gap is the real finding. The 9 published Ohio facilities sum to 118.4 MW, so this single campus is close to 30 percent of the state's known total. Ohio's data center footprint is largely invisible at the level of power, which means any statewide capacity estimate rests on a small and possibly unrepresentative sample.

The 35 MW is IT load, not a rack count. The operator publishes no rack count and no per-rack density, so the number of accelerators the campus could hold depends on an assumption the data does not supply. At 40 kW per rack it would be roughly 875 racks, but that is arithmetic on an assumed density, not a fact about the site. What the spec does establish is that the campus has both the power and the floor space for a substantial compute footprint.

The certifications, SOC 2 Type 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FISMA, SSAE 16 Type II, and Green Globes, qualify the campus for regulated workloads across finance, health, and federal categories. None names a tenant. The data does not say which accelerators, if any, run there, who leases the space, or what the campus pays for power, and those are the facts that would settle whether it matters to AI rather than to Ohio's power ledger.
